highlights.title: AI staff 'genuinely frightened' for humanity's future, ex-Anthropic researcher tells BBC
highlights.summary: It comes as the AI firm's boss has called for the technology's development to be slowed down, citing "serious" risks.
body: An artificial intelligence researcher who quit AI firm Anthropic has said people working on the technology were "genuinely frightened" about the speed of its advancements and what it could mean for humanity.
"I believe that if we don't slow down at the current rate of progress, there is a strong chance that we could all die in the immediate future," he said.
Jacob Coxon was speaking to the BBC after his resignation post on the dangers of AI went viral on a backdrop of growing safety concerns about the industry.
The 27-year-old's former boss, Anthropic head Dario Amodei, recently called for AI development to slow down - though some have questioned the motivations behind this.

highlights.title: Perplexity trusts GPT-6 Astra with end-to-end systems
highlights.summary: Perplexity uses Astra to write communications, change software, and monitor production systems, and checks in much less frequently than with earlier models.
body: As an AI-powered answer engine, Perplexity is deeply focused on search and accuracy. Its ability to process large amounts of information is critically important. Johnny Ho, Cofounder and Chief Strategy Officer, observes that every time the model gets better at writing code, Perplexity’s search engine improves too. It becomes able to write better programs that search the web and internal information and summarize it very concisely.
But the real challenge, according to Johnny, is taking those informational aspects and applying them to real-world systems. Something made easier with GPT‑6 Astra.
For Johnny, one of the most useful applications of AI is testing code. With limited time to test manually, he asks GPT‑6 Astra to build a small testing program around an application.

The model generates realistic responses like those another service would send, for example, a language model API or a connector. By standing in for those services, the model can check how the application responds and test the workflow from start to finish.

highlights.title: Antonelli wins Spanish GP after luckless Norris loses out
highlights.summary: Kimi Antonelli took another step in his quest towards winning the 2026 world championship by benefitting from pit-stop misfortune for Lando Norris to win the first Spanish Grand Prix at the Madring.
body: McLaren's Norris had looked in control of the race after converting his superb pole position into a comfortable early race lead but the battle for victory turned on a lap-15 Virtual Safety Car when Aston Martin's Lance Stroll stopped in a run-off area.
With a VSC offering the field the chance of a so-called 'cheap' pit stop, McLaren were unable to pit Norris immediately as the Briton had just passed the pit-lane entry road.

But the following Antonelli and Verstappen had not, allowing Mercedes and Red Bull to pit their drivers respectively while Norris was running to a controlled reduced speed on track while marshals moved Stroll's car.

McLaren did pit Norris at the end of the next lap but, by then, the VSC had ended, meaning the field was back up to racing speed, with the misfortune then compounded by a slow seven-second service at his tyre change.

highlights.title: Netflix’s Biggest Cyberpunk Series Is Doing Something Completely Different in Season 2
highlights.summary: That philosophy comes from new series director Kai Ikarashi, who served as storyboard artist and animation director on season 1’s “Girl on Fire.” His use of light helped make it one of the series’ most visually distinctive and memorable episodes.
body: There is no light at the end of the tunnel in Night City. In Cyberpunk: Edgerunners 2, light isn’t a symbol of hope at all. It’s just another overwhelming force bearing down on the people who live hard lives in an even harder city.
“Rather than using light as something that connects us to the outside world, I used it as something that blocks it off,” Ikarashi tells Polygon. “I depicted light not as hope, but simply as a force.”

Released in 2022, the original Cyberpunk: Edgerunners combines Studio Trigger’s flashy animation with the oppressive dystopia of CD Projekt Red’s Cyberpunk 2077. The story follows David Martinez (Zach Aguilar), a teenager who installs a powerful military implant called the Sandevistan and joins a crew of mercenaries — only to lose his sense of self as he replaces more and more of his body with cyberware. That arc ultimately transforms his charming but strained love story with netrunner Lucy into a tragic one. The neon-soaked Night City is colorful and exciting, but it’s a brutal place that more often than not consumes anyone who tries to rise above their station.

highlights.title: My deep fryer lives in a tool polycule. Here’s how to stop buying things your friends already own
highlights.summary: The key to happiness isn’t hoarding gadgets – it’s loaning them out and buying fewer things. Sign up for the Filter US newsletter, your weekly guide to buying fewer, better things.
body: They live under your bed and in your basement, your garage and probably in that weird cabinet above the fridge that requires a stepstool.

Alton Brown calls them unitaskers: the tools and appliances that aspire to do only one thing and do it well. Pasta makers and juicers are the classics, but they exist outside the kitchen, too. Do you really need to own a post-hole digger? Seasonal candle molds?

Well yes, sometimes. Which is why so many of us have them lurking in the recesses of our homes and apartments, gathering dust while they wait for the next dinner party that requires homemade ravioli. Local tool libraries solve this problem for home projects by filling shelves with borrowable tools instead of books. But if you don’t have one near you, or just tasks beyond DIY, I have a solution anyone can try: start a tool polycule.

For years now, half a dozen friends and I have operated an informal group here in Portland, Oregon, that swaps all the insipid items that spend 364 days a year sitting unused. It’s less a library than a group of people taking a nonmonogamous view of products instead of partners (though that type of polycule is popular in Portland, too).

highlights.summary: In May, hundreds of malicious and spam packages were uploaded to RubyGems, causing a serious disruption for the host. Now independent researchers have said that a swarm of OpenAI agents were responsible for the attack. Not only that, but the AI tried to steal users' API keys.
body: The previously undisclosed attack on Ruby Gems predates Hugging Face by more than a month.

The agents in this instance managed to bypass RubyGems’ email verification system to create a large number of accounts, then overwhelmed it with submissions. It then used the site’s automatic build system to remotely execute code and tried to exploit a vulnerability to steal user API keys. Though, it’s unclear if it ever succeeded.

Typically, this is when things get really interesting, especially in video games, where the sprint toward holiday sales may not have quite the same emphasis it did 20 years ago, but is still hardly vestigial. Especially when the looming colossus of Grand Theft Auto 6 moves the finish line forward for everyone else ( except Nintendo ).

In Polygon's fall preview this week, we've been rooting around for stories to sharpen your appetite for the season ahead, from talking to Zach Cregger about his Resident Evil movie to talking to talking to the makers of Ace Combat 8 about the art of video game clouds. And hey, did you remember that Gears of War: E-Day is a thing? For some reason, I keep forgetting.

highlights.title: Elkie Brooks looks back: ‘Before I went on stage I used to drink Guinness and a few shots of brandy’
highlights.summary: The singer-songwriter on her rock’n’roll past, playing second fiddle to the Beatles, and the key to being an energetic performer in your 80s. Born Elaine Bookbinder in Salford in 1945, Elkie Brooks is a rock, blues and jazz singer known as the British Queen of Blues.
body: This is me in a white jumpsuit outside the Royal Albert Hall in London. I have very few memories of the gig, but I know I would have felt daunted as it’s such a large venue. To overcome the nerves, I’d have tried to focus on the music and remembered, “It’s just another gig.”

Ever since I can remember, I have been singing, often in the bath, to my mummy. When I was seven I would get invited to sing Mr Sandman with the band that would play at weddings and barmitzvahs. As I got older, I adored Johnnie Ray and Ella Fitzgerald, then Billie Holiday, Sarah Vaughan, Dakota Staton, Esther Phillips and Aretha Franklin. The cantor at the local synagogue used to give me singing lessons, all in Hebrew and Yiddish. He was the one who taught me the correct way to project my voice.

highlights.title: We Need More Games Like Echo Weaver
highlights.summary: Echo Weaver is a platformer due to arrive next month from Moonlight Kids, known for 2021 hit The Wild at Heart. It’s also a Metroidvania that feels a bit like a roguelite, but with more emphasis on puzzles and hand-crafted stages.
body: The game begins by dropping the player character into an alien environment and setting them free to explore until they either die or run out of time. Whatever they discover, that’s the fruit of a single “cycle.” Then they reappear to attempt some of the same things again in the familiar corridors (stages are handcrafted, not procedurally-generated), while relying on knowledge gleaned from their previous runs. As play progresses, the world they know naturally expands. They find ways to push further in all directions, and to unearth secrets about the mysterious complex that contains them. In the process, they might even learn new things about themselves.
Chris Sumsky, game designer, programmer, and Moonlight Kids co-founder, recalled some of the thinking behind the game’s design, which takes cues from the 2019 indie hit Outer Wilds.

“There are time loop games, of course,” Sumsky told Polygon, “not least of which the very one we were inspired by. There are knowledge-gated games, not many, but they’re gaining popularity. And naturally, there are platformers. Many… many platformers. But we weren’t seeing anyone really combining all these into one.”

highlights.title: Ali Asgari Doesn’t Believe in a Bright Future After Iran’s January Massacre – Just ‘A Bit of Light’
highlights.summary: Iranian director Ali Asgari has no desire to repeat clichés about great expectations for things to come. “In Iran, we don’t have high hopes for the future anymore,” he states. “We’ve been waiting for good news for so many years, and it never came. But I do believe in these small specks of light. For
body: “Right now, especially in my country, we are forgetting about them. We’re forgetting about our families and helping others. We are surrounded by disaster every day, all the time, always expecting something horrible to happen,” he says.

“When we wake up, we don’t know if we’ll be able to handle it until nighttime. We’re all living in a dangerous world right now. If after watching this film someone goes to their mother and takes her hand, that’s enough.”

Family is certainly on the mind of his protagonist, a kind doctor (played by Misagh Zareh) who becomes disillusioned after his arrest. With his medical practice shut down, he’s ready to end his life. He’s a practical man, though, so he decides to tell his family and make suitable arrangements.
“Some doctors in Iran were the only witnesses to what was really happening after the massacre in January. They faced so much death and saw so many injured. We couldn’t even talk about it,” he notes.

highlights.title: Anthropic CEO says it’s time to pump the brakes on AI
highlights.summary: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei says the time has come to slow down AI development and will give third-party evaluators like METR access to its models to help ensure its "adherence to safety practices and commitments." In a winding essay, Amodei proposed a three-step plan to "pace the frontier" - jargon…
body: Dario Amodei proposed a three-step plan to ‘pace the frontier’ of AI development.

Amodei says that giving external evaluators wide-ranging access is just the first step, and one it is taking now unilaterally. Step two would involve the industry coming together as a whole, likely with government agencies to “establish common safety standards as well as limits on the rate of unchecked AI progress.” This step would focus on AI companies operating in democratic countries, but because passing laws and building regulatory infrastructure takes time, Amodei says that the industry should work together to create safety standards.

The third step would be the most challenging — getting authoritarian governments like those in China and Russia to agree to slow development and adopt a global set of AI safety standards. But he also says it’s crucial that the US and other democracies maintain a technological lead over China and other authoritarian regimes by limiting their access to high-powered chips and cracking down on things like distillation that allow companies to quickly catch up by training its AI to replicate the behavior of a more powerful model.

highlights.title: OpenAI boss and Elon Musk back calls to put brakes on ‘reckless’ AI development
highlights.summary: Rare show of unity from rival developers after safety warnings from Anthropic boss and AI researchers. The Guardian view on controlling AI: humanity cannot outsource its survival.
body: Sam Altman and Elon Musk have backed a call from the head of Anthropic, Dario Amodei, to “slow the pace” of AI development after he warned that an AI swarm could otherwise become capable of “taking over the entire internet” within a year.

In a rare show of unity, the rival technology leaders threw their weight behind the appeal from the founder and chief executive of the artificial intelligence company Anthropic, which came after a series of warnings from AI researchers last week.

In an essay, Amodei laid out his thoughts on “why the AI industry should slow down”, with a three-part plan for doing so, starting with giving independent monitors constant access to developers’ research processes. Amodei said “building [AI] too fast is reckless” and he feared that after hundreds of OpenAI agents hacked into the Hugging Face website this summer, a swarm with greater capabilities but similarly misaligned could cause hundreds of billions of dollars of damage by “taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet”. This was disputed by some AI experts as not particularly plausible and to be treated with scepticism.

highlights.summary: Star turns in 'Hit & Run,' 'From' and 'The Betrayers' thriller this year at the Toronto Film Festival have got Ohm onto everyone's call sheets in Canada.
body: Kaelen Ohm says what got her as a fearless young skier better and faster down mountains in small-town Canada now drives her climb onto everyone’s call sheets as a go-for-it actor, filmmaker and musician.

That need to go her own way as an actor and artist over two decades includes early TV roles in Hell on Wheels, Taken and Murdoch Mysteries. “Often you are playing against a show’s leads, so I got to walk in and watch Brendan Fraser work for a day,” Ohm recalls of a one-episode stint on Condor alongside the Oscar-winning The Whale star.

Ohm’s breakout TV role came in 2020 as Danielle, a gifted American dancer killed in a car accident in the first episode of Netflix’s bingeable mystery Hit & Run. Her husband, played by Fauda star Lior Raz, then investigates her unexplained death as Ohm’s character appears in flashbacks.

“That was an act of God,” she says of first auditioning for Raz and The Killing and The Handmaid’s Tale creators in New York City. “I thought I’m going to meet these incredible creatives with decades-long careers and I was the least nervous I’d ever been because I thought there’s no way this will work out for me.”

highlights.title: How to make chocolate mousse – recipe | Felicity Cloake's Masterclass
highlights.summary: The little black dress of desserts, this French staple is quick and easy to make, and almost always delivers. Experiment with flavours and toppings to put your own spin on a classic.
body: Years ago, a group of us cycled from Brittany to the Mediterranean, and along the way we ate a lot of chocolate mousse. Popular, easy to make and happy to sit in the fridge until required, it’s a mainstay of the modest French provincial restaurant and, as we discovered, it’s almost always good. Here’s my favourite version of the little black dress of the dessert trolley.

You can use milk or flavoured chocolate here, if you like, but do bear in mind that if it’s quite sweet, you probably won’t need the extra sugar. Unless you’re using uniform chocolate drops designed for melting, roughly chop the chocolate – there’s no need to cut it into very tiny pieces, but they should be fairly even so they melt at the same rate.

Boil the kettle. Meanwhile, get ready a large heatproof bowl that can sit over a pan holding about 5cm of water without the base of the bowl touching the water. Pour the boiling water into the pan and turn on the heat to medium. Put the chocolate in the bowl, then put the bowl on top of the water pan and turn down the heat so the water is barely simmering. Stir occasionally, until the chocolate is completely melted.

highlights.title: Trump is giving data centers a pass to pollute
highlights.summary: President Donald Trump is weakening environmental regulations in the name of speeding up the construction of AI data centers, raising health risks for Americans, a cadre of former EPA officials said this week in a briefing and new report.
body: The Trump administration is sacrificing Americans’ health to build data centers, former EPA officials warn.

At the start of his term, Trump’s EPA administrator, Lee Zeldin, proclaimed his goal of making America “ the AI capital of the world ” through deregulation. Since then, Zeldin and the White House have rolled back dozens of rules on top of cutting staff and funding at the US EPA.

As a result of the Trump administration’s deregulation spree and attacks on renewable energy, the wave of new AI data centers is increasingly powered by dirty energy that can impact Americans’ health even if they don’t live near a data center, the group of EPA alumni warn. They say that the agency they once worked for, which was created to “ protect human health and the environment,” is no longer the watchdog it should be as the physical infrastructure underpinning generative AI changes America’s landscape.
“You would think that an industry buildout of this magnitude, billed as a revolution, would mean more vigilance from EPA.”

highlights.title: Burning Man at 40: the once anarchic desert festival faces a midlife crisis
highlights.summary: The subversive bacchanal for San Francisco’s eccentric underground is ageing out amid an influx of the super-rich. Burning Man, the infamous arts festival in the Nevada desert, turned 40 this year, and it’s showing some distinct signs of middle age.
body: It’s not just the tech billionaires who show up to party, the chartered flights straight to the desert or the HBO documentary about behind-the-scenes power struggles. The tens of thousands of people who assemble each year to create a tent city in the wilderness appear to be growing older, and it doesn’t seem that they’re being replaced by as many younger “burners”, as festival participants are called.

People in their 20s used to make up nearly a third of the participants in this utopian experiment, in which volunteers build a new version of Black Rock City in the desert each year, party nonstop for a week and then burn much of the art they have created, including a massive effigy of the “Man.”

highlights.title: Diablo 4's new season brings back Deckard Cain and all three Prime Evils as the game arrives on Switch 2
highlights.summary: Diablo 4 's next season, Season of Hell's Legacy, will go live on 15th September to celebrate the franchise's 30th anniversary and Nintendo Switch 2 debut.
body: At BlizzCon's opening ceremony, developer Blizzard said the season will be a tribute to three decades of Diablo, built around the return of Deckard Cain and a rematch against all three original Prime Evils: Diablo, Baal, and Mephisto.

Cain's spirit returns to warn players that echoes of the three Prime Evils have resurfaced. Each one's holed up in a location familiar to those who've played the earlier games - Tristram Cathedral, Arreat Summit, the Durance of Hate. Beat one and you get a Soul Splinter, which lets you borrow a bit of that demon's power. The catch is that it also makes you more vulnerable to that same demon.

That's not all, either. Nine new Legacy Uniques also join the game permanently, including a returning Stone of Jordan, alongside a batch of enemy encounters called Waking Nightmares that recreate specific moments from Diablo's past.
The new content is slated to go live at 5.30pm UK time on 15th September.

highlights.title: OpenAI’s Sam Altman says it would be ‘ill-advised’ to go public in 2026
highlights.summary: While OpenAI has filed confidentially for an IPO, the company will not be going public this year, according to CEO Sam Altman.
body: Altman was interviewed recently by Fortune editor in chief Alyson Shontell; amidst the fallout from the OpenAI-HuggingFace hack, as well as broader discussions about AI safety, Shontell asked whether OpenAI still feels pressure to “move really fast” due to its IPO plans.
“We’re not rushing into an IPO,” Altman said. “I actually think that given everything happening with safety, right now would be an ill-advised moment to go public.”

Instead, he insisted that OpenAI will go public “when we’re ready, which is when the business is ready, when we feel ready from what the moment is like in society with this technology.” When pressed on whether that means the IPO isn’t happening in 2026, Altman replied, “I would say not 2026, yeah. We’ve got a lot of stuff to do.”

The New York Times reported in June that although OpenAI had hired bankers and lawyers with the goal of going public in the third or fourth quarter of 2026, the company was leaning toward 2027 due to the volatility of tech stocks and its own financial challenges.

highlights.summary: Blizzard has officially confirmed World of Warcraft: Forever, the long-rumoured "Classic+" experience.
body: Last week, World of Warcraft fans were obsessing over colours as dataminers pulled hues from Blizzard's website that were labelled under a curious "wow 2" tag, leading many to speculate that this referred to the rumoured World of Warcraft Camelot, or as it's better known, "Classic Plus", much like how Blizzard is now expanding Diablo 2.
Now, following BlizzCon's opening ceremony, it turns out the rumours were pretty much bang on and World of Warcraft: Forever launches globally on 4th November.
If November sounds very far away, worry not; beta access begins this Thursday, 17th September, for anyone who's pre-purchased one of the game's upgrade packs.

A dedicated panel featuring senior game director Ion Hazzikostas, lead Classic designer Tim Jones, lead software engineer Nora Mills, and associate production director Clay Stone went into more detail on the new regions, systems, and design philosophy behind the project.

highlights.title: ‘Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother’ Review: Mahershala Ali Is a Marvel in a Gripping Crime Film With a Big, Aching Heart
highlights.summary: The two-time Oscar winner plays a devout Muslim and contract killer forced to care for his three kids after his wife dies in Bassam Tariq's Texas-set thriller.
body: Latif is a strong, quiet man and lethal with a knife, but he’s also a father. When his wife Khadijah (Shakirah DeMesier) suddenly dies, leaving him as the sole parent of his three children, his work and family life collide. Soon he has to answer to Fatiha (Adia), his thoughtful and intelligent adolescent daughter, who challenges him with questions he doesn’t want to answer. His devout son Qadir (Jahleel Kamara) — still full of the energy and optimism of childhood — forces Latif to confront his lapsed faith. Then there’s Aziza, a nursing baby robbed of both the nourishment and comfort of her mother.

Latif must change his priorities rapidly. Suddenly, life for him becomes a constant search for breast milk to feed his daughter. Fatiha tries to give her sister formula, but the baby can’t digest it. Her constant hunger is a living manifestation of Latif’s inability to take his wife’s place. More comfortable in the role of provider, Latif has to learn how to tap into his nurturing side. Writer and director Bassam Tariq gives us a figure rarely seen on American screens: a Black Muslim man portrayed tenderly, with his family and faith as an anchor.
points: The two-time Oscar winner plays a devout Muslim and contract killer forced to care for his three kids after his wife dies in Bassam Tariq's Texas-set thriller.

But quick doesn’t have to mean boring. These easy 30-minute meals include spicy chicken lettuce wraps, sizzling shrimp fajitas, creamy carbonara, crispy tofu with peanut sauce, and plenty of one-pan dinners that minimize cleanup. Some lean on smart shortcuts like rotisserie chicken, canned tuna, or store-bought dumplings; others take advantage of naturally quick-cooking ingredients like shrimp, ground meat, tofu, and eggs.
Every recipe here can be made in 30 minutes or less, start to finish. Really pressed for time? Our 15-minute meals round-up includes even speedier options.
